**设计建议与待验证事项**：阅读位置可以由来源对象、内容锚点和局部偏移共同表达。仅保存像素值，在字体大小、容器宽度或内容高度改变后，可能对应不同文字；只保存行号，也可能丢失长段中的局部位置。应区分来源面板位置与正文位置，避免一个区域更新触发另一区域的自动跟随。实际验证可以观察用户上滚、展开来源、返回正文等动作后，同一段是否仍可继续阅读，并区分用户主动导航和系统自动移动。本次没有运行这些动作，无法评价现有行为是否满足目标。

## 5. 流式正文：继续生成与自动跟随应分别表达

**设计建议**：第4行支持讨论“阅读来源时后文继续生成”的目标，但没有提供实现符号、状态机或性能记录。产品可以将生成过程与视口跟随视为不同状态：后台仍接收正文，并不意味着用户必须随新内容滚动。用户离开末尾阅读旧内容时，新增内容提示可能比强制滚到底部更合适；用户主动选择回到末尾时，再恢复跟随。具体策略属于设计选择，不是本地输入规定的唯一解法。

**设计建议**：流式正文可能先出现论述，再出现引用入口；也可能先显示待确认标记，随后补充可打开的来源。两种顺序都需要让用户区分“已有正文”和“来源已可访问”。本次第2行提出准确命中行，第4行提出持续生成与阅读位置目标，但三条输入均未描述实际引用生成协议。因此，引用异步补齐只是需要讨论的设计情境，不能被当成对现有架构的观察结论。

**文档事实**：页面 “Success Criterion” 部分的条件是：当网页可以顺序导航，且导航顺序影响意义或操作时，可聚焦组件应按保持意义和可操作性的顺序获得焦点。“Intent” 进一步解释，合理顺序可能不止一种，例如表格按行或按列遍历，都可能反映内容关系。这意味着判断重点是用户能否理解和操作，而不是所有页面必须采用同一条焦点路线。

**适用边界与设计建议**：对于正文、引用入口和 Sources 子侧栏，应先识别它们的逻辑关系，再决定导航顺序。不能只因侧栏位于右侧，就宣布它必须最后获得焦点；也不能因引用靠近某句话，就要求每个正文段落都加入 Tab 顺序。建议把“阅读论述—打开相关来源—操作来源—继续阅读”作为候选任务路径，检查布局和导航是否支持它。本次未读取产品 DOM 或实际按键，因此无法判定现有顺序是否合理，更没有 WCAG 符合性结论。

## 8. 视觉位置与阅读顺序：允许差异，但不能破坏理解

**文档事实**：“Intent” 明确指出，焦点顺序不必与程序确定的阅读顺序完全相同，只要用户仍能理解和操作页面；也不必机械遵循视觉布局。页面用独立双栏说明，先遍历右栏再遍历左栏未必构成失败，同时把强化视觉布局暗示的阅读顺序称为最佳实践。它提醒作者同时考虑屏幕阅读器用户和能够看见页面的键盘用户，避免让其中一类用户感到焦点随机跳转。

**设计建议与待验证事项**：Sources 与正文在视觉上相邻，不代表它们在辅助技术读取或顺序导航中也相邻。建议为区域提供清楚的名称和关系，使用户理解自己从哪里进入、当前操作什么、如何返回。后续需分别观察视觉键盘路径与程序确定的阅读路径，而不能只看鼠标操作截图。即使视觉上没有移动，焦点也可能已经转移；即使滚动到了目标行，键盘也可能仍停留在旧入口。这些是需要分开检查的状态，不是本次已经发现的缺陷。

## 9. 来源面板的交互类型：不能凭“侧栏”二字推导焦点规则

**文档事实**：“Examples” 分别给出非模态与模态对话框示例。非模态示例把对话框内交互元素放在触发按钮之后的焦点顺序中；模态示例则在打开后将焦点置于内部，使外部网页内容不可获得焦点，关闭后返回触发按钮或其后元素。这些例子解释了交互关系如何影响焦点组织，不是在规定所有展开区域都必须成为模态对话框。

**设计建议与待验证事项**：本地第4行希望用户阅读来源时正文继续生成，但它没有规定面板属于模态还是非模态。后台生成继续，与用户能否操作面板外部，是两个不同问题。建议根据实际任务选择交互类型：若希望随时在正文和来源之间操作，应评估非模态方案；若确有独占操作需求，则应明确说明其边界。后续验证需检查打开、关闭、重复切换以及触发入口消失后的焦点去向，不能直接把官方示例复制成未经验证的产品要求。

**文档事实**：页面说明动态 HTML 可以通过脚本和 `tabindex` 改变导航顺序；其技术列表也列出把动态内容插入触发元素之后的技术。不过页面明确说，列出的技术可能超过最低要求，也可能存在其他满足方式。因此不能把某种 DOM 插入位置宣称为全部产品必须使用的唯一方案，更不能从技术列表推导出具体流式更新架构。

**设计建议与待验证事项**：正文生成期间补齐引用，可能使新的可聚焦入口出现在用户当前焦点之前或之后。建议检查用户继续按 Tab 时，是否仍能理解下一步去了哪里，而不是仅检查入口数量增加。来源阅读时避免无理由抢走焦点，也是值得评估的策略，但它不等于“所有更新都禁止焦点变化”。由用户明确发起的导航可能需要转移焦点；被动接收文字则未必需要。区分触发原因、目标对象和当前阅读任务，比一概移动或一概不移动更有解释力。

**文档事实**：页面 “Note” 明确说明，该要求评估的是获得焦点的顺序，不规定哪些内容应该或不应该获得焦点。静态文字可以获得焦点，也可以被程序移入焦点；但若产生妨碍理解、操作或混乱的顺序，则可能失败。页面以可聚焦容器嵌套按钮为例，说明一个控件看起来多次获得焦点的风险，并将避免不可操作的焦点项称为最佳实践。

**设计建议与待验证事项**：来源行号和长路径不应仅为了“键盘能够读到”而全部变成连续 Tab 停靠点，否则用户可能需要穿越大量没有操作意义的项目。可以区分打开、复制、关闭等交互控件与供阅读的文本，再根据实际任务决定是否需要程序聚焦目标行。后续应检查同一来源卡片是否因容器和内部按钮而出现难以理解的重复停靠，以及路径信息是否可由键盘获取。本次既未观察控件结构，也未使用辅助技术，不能宣称存在重复焦点或信息不可访问。

What to do Elements receive focus in an order that preserves meaning. Why it's important Navigating a site or application with only the keyboard will make sense. ## Success Criterion (SC) If a [web page](#dfn-web-page) can be [navigated sequentially](#dfn-navigated-sequentially) and the navigation sequences affect meaning or operation, focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability. ## Intent The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that when users navigate sequentially through content, they encounter information in an order that is consistent with the meaning of the content and can be operated from the keyboard. This reduces confusion by letting users form a consistent mental model of the content. There may be different orders that reflect logical relationships in the content. For example, moving through components in a table one row at a time or one column at a time both reflect the logical relationships in the content. Either order may satisfy this success criterion. The way that sequential navigation order is determined in web content is defined by the technology of the content. For example, simple HTML defines sequential navigation via the notion of tabbing order. Dynamic HTML may modify the navigation sequence using scripting along with the addition of a `tabindex` attribute to allow focus to additional elements. If no scripting or `tabindex` attributes are used, the navigation order is the order that components appear in the content stream. (See [Focus in the HTML Living Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#focus)). An example of keyboard navigation that is not the sequential navigation addressed by this success criterion is using arrow key navigation to traverse a tree component. The user can use the up and down arrow keys to move from tree node to tree node. Pressing the right arrow key may expand a node, then using the down arrow key, will move into the newly expanded nodes. This navigation sequence follows the expected sequence for a tree control - as additional items get expanded or collapsed, they are added or removed from the navigation sequence. The focus order may not be identical to the programmatically determined reading order (see [Success Criterion 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence](meaningful-sequence.html)) as long as the user can still understand and operate the web page. Since there may be several possible logical reading orders for the content, the focus order may match any of them. However, when the order of a particular presentation differs from the programmatically determined reading order, users of one of these presentations may find it difficult to understand or operate the web page. Authors should carefully consider all these users as they design their web pages. For example, a screen reader user interacts with the programmatically determined reading order, while a sighted keyboard user interacts with the visual presentation of the web page. Care should be taken so that the focus order makes sense to both of these sets of users and does not appear to either of them to jump around randomly. Focus order needs to allow the user to navigate focusable elements in a logical order, and that order needs to preserve any meaning or operation that the page is conveying. Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual layout of the web page, as long as the order in which elements receive focus is logical, and the hierarchy and relationship of content implied by the visual presentation is preserved. For instance, in a two-column layout, the assumption in western left-to-right systems may be that focus moves through the elements in the left-hand column first, from the top to the bottom of the column, and then proceed to the right-hand column. However, if the two columns are independent of each other, and meaning/operation are not affected, it is not a failure if elements in the right-hand column receive focus first, followed by the elements in the left-hand column. As a best practice, though, make sure the focus order reinforces the reading order implied by the visual layout. Note This requirement does not specify what should or should not receive focus, but rather assesses the order in which elements receive focus. This success criterion does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable, or programmatically moving focus to such content. However, it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements. ```html
``` As a best practice, avoid having focusable elements which cannot be operated or actioned, as these are likely to make operation tedious for keyboard users. For clarity: - Focusable components need to receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability. - Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual presentation or layout. - If there is more than one order that preserves meaning and operability, only one of them needs to be provided. - Static/non-interactive elements can receive focus, as long as they don't impede operation of the content, or result in confusing or illogical focus order. ## Benefits These techniques benefit keyboard users who navigate documents sequentially and expect the focus order to be consistent with the sequential reading order. - People with mobility impairments who must rely on keyboard access for operating a page benefit from a logical, usable focus order. - People with disabilities that make reading difficult can become disoriented when tabbing takes focus someplace unexpected. They benefit from a logical focus order. - People with visual impairments can become disoriented when tabbing takes focus someplace unexpected or when they cannot easily find the content surrounding an interactive element. - Only a small portion of the page may be visible to an individual using a screen magnifier at a high level of magnification. Such a user may interpret a field in the wrong context if the focus order is not logical. ## Examples - On a web page that contains a tree of interactive controls, the user can use the up and down arrow keys to move from tree node to tree node. Pressing the right arrow key expands a node, then using the down arrow key moves into the newly expanded nodes. - A web page implements non-modal dialogs. When the trigger button is activated, a dialog opens. The interactive elements in the dialog are inserted in the focus order immediately after the button. When the dialog is open, the focus order goes from the button to the elements of the dialog, then to the interactive element following the button. When the dialog is closed, the focus order goes from the button to the following element. - A web page implements modal dialogs. When the trigger button is activated, a dialog opens and focus is set within the dialog. As long as the dialog is open, all web page content outside the dialog becomes inert and cannot receive focus (though, depending on implementation, the focus cycle might still include user agent controls). When the dialog is dismissed, focus returns to the button or the element following the button. - An HTML web page is created with the left hand navigation occurring in the HTML after the main body content, and styled with CSS to appear on the left hand side of the page. This is done to allow focus to move to the main body content first without requiring `tabindex` attributes or JavaScript. Note While this example passes the Success Criterion, it is not necessarily true that all CSS positioning would. More complex positioning examples may or may not preserve meaning and operability - The following example **fails to meet the Success Criterion**: A company's website includes a form that collects marketing data and allows users to subscribe to several newsletters published by the company. The section of the form for collecting marketing data includes fields such as name, street address, city, state or province, and postal code. Another section of the form includes several checkboxes so that users can indicate newsletters they want to receive. However, the tab order for the form skips between fields in different sections of the form, so that focus moves from the name field to a checkbox, then to the street address, then to another checkbox. ## Techniques Each item in this section represents a technique or combination of techniques that the Accessibility Guidelines Working Group deems sufficient for meeting this success criterion.       "content": "Understanding Success Criterion 2.4.3: Focus Order | WAI | W3C    [Skip to content](#main)\n\n[WCAG 2.2 Understanding Docs](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/)\n\nInformative explanations, not required to meet WCAG\n\n[About WCAG Understanding Docs](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/about)\n\n[W3C homepage](https://www.w3.org/) [Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) homepage](https://www.w3.org/WAI/)\n\n-   [All Understanding Docs](.)\n-   [Guideline: Navigable](navigable)\n-   [Previous SC: Page Titled](page-titled)\n-   [Next SC: Link Purpose (In Context)](link-purpose-in-context)\n\nPage Contents\n\n-   [In Brief](#brief)\n-   [Success Criterion](#success-criterion)\n-   [Intent](#intent)\n-   [Benefits](#benefits)\n-   [Examples](#examples)\n-   [Techniques](#techniques)\n-   [Key Terms](#key-terms)\n\n# Understanding [SC 2.4.3](https://w3.org/TR/WCAG22#focus-order) Focus Order (Level A)\n\n## In Brief\n\nGoal\n\nKeyboard users navigate content in a correct order.\n\nWhat to do\n\nElements receive focus in an order that preserves meaning.\n\nWhy it's important\n\nNavigating a site or application with only the keyboard will make sense.\n\n## Success Criterion (SC)\n\nIf a [web page](#dfn-web-page) can be [navigated sequentially](#dfn-navigated-sequentially) and the navigation sequences affect meaning or operation, focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability.\n\n## Intent\n\nThe intent of this success criterion is to ensure that when users navigate sequentially through content, they encounter information in an order that is consistent with the meaning of the content and can be operated from the keyboard. This reduces confusion by letting users form a consistent mental model of the content. There may be different orders that reflect logical relationships in the content. For example, moving through components in a table one row at a time or one column at a time both reflect the logical relationships in the content. Either order may satisfy this success criterion.\n\nThe way that sequential navigation order is determined in web content is defined by the technology of the content. For example, simple HTML defines sequential navigation via the notion of tabbing order. Dynamic HTML may modify the navigation sequence using scripting along with the addition of a `tabindex` attribute to allow focus to additional elements. If no scripting or `tabindex` attributes are used, the navigation order is the order that components appear in the content stream. (See [Focus in the HTML Living Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#focus)).\n\nAn example of keyboard navigation that is not the sequential navigation addressed by this success criterion is using arrow key navigation to traverse a tree component. The user can use the up and down arrow keys to move from tree node to tree node. Pressing the right arrow key may expand a node, then using the down arrow key, will move into the newly expanded nodes. This navigation sequence follows the expected sequence for a tree control - as additional items get expanded or collapsed, they are added or removed from the navigation sequence.\n\nThe focus order may not be identical to the programmatically determined reading order (see [Success Criterion 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence](meaningful-sequence.html)) as long as the user can still understand and operate the web page. Since there may be several possible logical reading orders for the content, the focus order may match any of them. However, when the order of a particular presentation differs from the programmatically determined reading order, users of one of these presentations may find it difficult to understand or operate the web page. Authors should carefully consider all these users as they design their web pages.\n\nFor example, a screen reader user interacts with the programmatically determined reading order, while a sighted keyboard user interacts with the visual presentation of the web page. Care should be taken so that the focus order makes sense to both of these sets of users and does not appear to either of them to jump around randomly.\n\nFocus order needs to allow the user to navigate focusable elements in a logical order, and that order needs to preserve any meaning or operation that the page is conveying. Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual layout of the web page, as long as the order in which elements receive focus is logical, and the hierarchy and relationship of content implied by the visual presentation is preserved. For instance, in a two-column layout, the assumption in western left-to-right systems may be that focus moves through the elements in the left-hand column first, from the top to the bottom of the column, and then proceed to the right-hand column. However, if the two columns are independent of each other, and meaning/operation are not affected, it is not a failure if elements in the right-hand column receive focus first, followed by the elements in the left-hand column. As a best practice, though, make sure the focus order reinforces the reading order implied by the visual layout.\n\nNote\n\nThis requirement does not specify what should or should not receive focus, but rather assesses the order in which elements receive focus. This success criterion does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable, or programmatically moving focus to such content. However, it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements.\n\n```html\n<div tabindex=\"0\"><button>...</button></div>\n```\n\nAs a best practice, avoid having focusable elements which cannot be operated or actioned, as these are likely to make operation tedious for keyboard users.\n\nFor clarity:\n\n-   Focusable components need to receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability.\n-   Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual presentation or layout.\n-   If there is more than one order that preserves meaning and operability, only one of them needs to be provided.\n-   Static/non-interactive elements can receive focus, as long as they don't impede operation of the content, or result in confusing or illogical focus order.\n\n## Benefits\n\nThese techniques benefit keyboard users who navigate documents sequentially and expect the focus order to be consistent with the sequential reading order.\n\n-   People with mobility impairments who must rely on keyboard access for operating a page benefit from a logical, usable focus order.\n-   People with disabilities that make reading difficult can become disoriented when tabbing takes focus someplace unexpected. They benefit from a logical focus order.\n-   People with visual impairments can become disoriented when tabbing takes focus someplace unexpected or when they cannot easily find the content surrounding an interactive element.\n-   Only a small portion of the page may be visible to an individual using a screen magnifier at a high level of magnification. Such a user may interpret a field in the wrong context if the focus order is not logical.\n\n## Examples\n\n-   On a web page that contains a tree of interactive controls, the user can use the up and down arrow keys to move from tree node to tree node. Pressing the right arrow key expands a node, then using the down arrow key moves into the newly expanded nodes.\n-   A web page implements non-modal dialogs. When the trigger button is activated, a dialog opens. The interactive elements in the dialog are inserted in the focus order immediately after the button. When the dialog is open, the focus order goes from the button to the elements of the dialog, then to the interactive element following the button. When the dialog is closed, the focus order goes from the button to the following element.\n-   A web page implements modal dialogs. When the trigger button is activated, a dialog opens and focus is set within the dialog. As long as the dialog is open, all web page content outside the dialog becomes inert and cannot receive focus (though, depending on implementation, the focus cycle might still include user agent controls). When the dialog is dismissed, focus returns to the button or the element following the button.\n-   An HTML web page is created with the left hand navigation occurring in the HTML after the main body content, and styled with CSS to appear on the left hand side of the page. This is done to allow focus to move to the main body content first without requiring `tabindex` attributes or JavaScript.\n\n    Note\n\n    While this example passes the Success Criterion, it is not necessarily true that all CSS positioning would. More complex positioning examples may or may not preserve meaning and operability\n\n-   The following example **fails to meet the Success Criterion**:\n\n    A company's website includes a form that collects marketing data and allows users to subscribe to several newsletters published by the company. The section of the form for collecting marketing data includes fields such as name, street address, city, state or province, and postal code. Another section of the form includes several checkboxes so that users can indicate newsletters they want to receive. However, the tab order for the form skips between fields in different sections of the form, so that focus moves from the name field to a checkbox, then to the street address, then to another checkbox.\n\n\n## Techniques\n\nEach item in this section represents a technique or combination of techniques that the Accessibility Guidelines Working Group deems sufficient for meeting this success criterion. A technique may go beyond the minimum requirement of the criterion. There may be other ways of meeting the criterion not covered by these techniques. For information on using other techniques, see [Understanding Techniques for WCAG Success Criteria](understanding-techniques), particularly the \"Other Techniques\" section.\n\n### Sufficient Techniques\n\n-   [G59: Placing the interactive elements in an order that follows sequences and relationships within the content](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/general/G59)\n-   Giving focus to elements in an order that follows sequences and relationships within the content using one of the following techniques:\n\n    -   [C27: Making the DOM order match the visual order](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/css/C27)\n    -   [PDF3: Ensuring correct tab and reading order in PDF documents](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/pdf/PDF3)\n-   Changing a web page dynamically using one of the following techniques:\n\n    -   [SCR26: Inserting dynamic content into the Document Object Model immediately following its trigger element](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/client-side-script/SCR26)\n    -   [H102: Creating modal dialogs with the HTML dialog element](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/html/H102)\n    -   [SCR27: Reordering page sections using the Document Object Model](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/client-side-script/SCR27)\n\n### Failures\n\nThe following are common mistakes that are considered failures of this success criterion by the Accessibility Guidelines Working Group.\n\n-   [F44: Failure of Success Criterion 2.4.3 due to using tabindex to create a tab order that does not preserve meaning and operability](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/failures/F44)\n-   [F85: Failure of Success Criterion 2.4.3 due to using dialogs or menus that are not adjacent to their trigger control in the sequential navigation order](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/failures/F85)\n\n## Key Terms\n\nassistive technology\n\nhardware and/or software that acts as a [user agent](#dfn-user-agent), or along with a mainstream user agent, to provide functionality to meet the requirements of users with disabilities that go beyond those offered by mainstream user agents\n\nNote 1\n\nFunctionality provided by assistive technology includes alternative presentations (e.g., as synthesized speech or magnified content), alternative input methods (e.g., voice), additional navigation or orientation mechanisms, and content transformations (e.g., to make tables more accessible).\n\nNote 2\n\nAssistive technologies often communicate data and messages with mainstream user agents by using and monitoring APIs.\n\nNote 3\n\nThe distinction between mainstream user agents and assistive technologies is not absolute. Many mainstream user agents provide some features to assist individuals with disabilities. The basic difference is that mainstream user agents target broad and diverse audiences that usually include people with and without disabilities. Assistive technologies target narrowly defined populations of users with specific disabilities. The assistance provided by an assistive technology is more specific and appropriate to the needs of its target users. The mainstream user agent may provide important functionality to assistive technologies like retrieving web content from program objects or parsing markup into identifiable bundles.\n\nExample\n\nAssistive technologies that are important in the context of this document include the following:\n\n-   screen magnifiers, and other visual reading assistants, which are used by people with visual, perceptual and physical print disabilities to change text font, size, spacing, color, synchronization with speech, etc. in order to improve the visual readability of rendered text and images;\n-   screen readers, which are used by people who are blind to read textual information through synthesized speech or braille;\n-   text-to-speech software, which is used by some people with cognitive, language, and learning disabilities to convert text into synthetic speech;\n-   speech recognition software, which may be used by people who have some physical disabilities;\n-   alternative keyboards, which are used by people with certain physical disabilities to simulate the keyboard (including alternate keyboards that use head pointers, single switches, sip/puff and other special input devices.);\n-   alternative pointing devices, which are used by people with certain physical disabilities to simulate mouse pointing and button activations.\n\nkeyboard interface\n\ninterface used by software to obtain keystroke input\n\nNote 1\n\nA keyboard interface allows users to provide keystroke input to programs even if the native technology does not contain a keyboard.\n\nExample\n\nA touchscreen PDA has a keyboard interface built into its operating system as well as a connector for external keyboards. Applications on the PDA can use the interface to obtain keyboard input either from an external keyboard or from other applications that provide simulated keyboard output, such as handwriting interpreters or speech-to-text applications with \"keyboard emulation\" functionality.\n\nNote 2\n\nOperation of the application (or parts of the application) through a keyboard-operated mouse emulator, such as MouseKeys, does not qualify as operation through a keyboard interface because operation of the program is through its pointing device interface, not through its keyboard interface.\n\nnavigated sequentially\n\nnavigated in the order defined for advancing focus (from one element to the next) using a [keyboard interface](#dfn-keyboard-interface)\n\nuser agent\n\nany software that retrieves and presents web content for users\n\nExample\n\nWeb browsers, media players, plug-ins, and other programs — including [assistive technologies](#dfn-assistive-technology) — that help in retrieving, rendering, and interacting with web content.\n\nweb page\n\na non-embedded resource obtained from a single URI using HTTP plus any other resources that are used in the rendering or intended to be rendered together with it by a [user agent](#dfn-user-agent)\n\nNote 1\n\nAlthough any \"other resources\" would be rendered together with the primary resource, they would not necessarily be rendered simultaneously with each other.\n\nNote 2\n\nFor the purposes of conformance with these guidelines, a resource must be \"non-embedded\" within the scope of conformance to be considered a web page.\n\nExample 1\n\nA web resource including all embedded images and media.\n\nExample 2\n\nA web mail program built using Asynchronous JavaScript and XML (AJAX). The program lives entirely at http://example.com/mail, but includes an inbox, a contacts area and a calendar. Links or buttons are provided that cause the inbox, contacts, or calendar to display, but do not change the URI of the page as a whole.\n\nExample 3\n\nA customizable portal site, where users can choose content to display from a set of different content modules.\n\nExample 4\n\nWhen you enter \"http://shopping.example.com/\" in your browser, you enter a movie-like interactive shopping environment where you visually move around in a store dragging products off of the shelves around you and into a visual shopping cart in front of you. Clicking on a product causes it to be demonstrated with a specification sheet floating alongside. This might be a single-page website or just one page within a website.\n\n[Back to Top](#top)\n\n## Help improve this page\n\nPlease share your ideas, suggestions, or comments via email to the publicly-archived list [public-agwg-comments@w3.org](mailto:public-agwg-comments@w3.org?subject=%5BUnderstanding%20and%20Techniques%20Feedback%5D) or via GitHub\n\n[Email](mailto:public-agwg-comments@w3.org?subject=%5BUnderstanding%20and%20Techniques%20Feedback%5D) [Fork & Edit on GitHub](https://github.com/w3c/wcag/edit/main/understanding/20/focus-order.html) [New GitHub Issue](https://github.com/w3c/wcag/issues/new)\n\n**Date:** Updated 09 March 2026.
